result:
**bridge.npz is saved** in this folder. M has shape 16 × 24, c has shape 24, and all values are finite. I couldn't measure B's accuracy with it, because the rules forbid running the networks on any input. So the scores below are analytical estimates, not test results.

**Construction.** The bridge is the best linear estimator of B's first-layer pre-activation, `z1B = x @ W0B + b0B`, given A's message `h1A = relu(x @ W0A + b0A)`.

- **Pixel prior.** I assumed a Gaussian distribution over pixels. It is spatially smooth and fixes the pixels that both networks ignore to zero.
- **Pooling.** I combined 24 versions of that prior, varying mean ink (0.2 / 0.35), spread (0.3 / 0.4), smoothness (length 0.7 / 1.0 / 1.5) and whether ink is flat or concentrated towards the centre.
- **No sampling.** The moments a linear estimator needs, such as `E[h1A h1Aᵀ]` and `Cov(h1A, z1B)`, came from exact formulas for rectified Gaussians. I checked the two-unit formula against numerical integration of a 2-D density. No image or input vector was sampled, built, or passed through either network.
- **Fit.** M and c come from a lightly ridge-regularised normal-equation solve on the pooled moments. A's dead unit 7 (all-zero weights, negative bias, so it always outputs 0) gets a zero row in M, so it has no effect.

**Why not the simplest approach.** A weights-only least-squares fit (`W0A @ M ≈ W0B`, `c = b0B − b0A @ M`) assumes all 16 of A's units are active. Under these priors each unit is active only 21–98% of the time, and that fit explained much less of z1B:

| Bridge | Mean R² across the 24 priors | Worst prior |
|---|---|---|
| Weights-only least squares | 0.54 | 0.36 |
| Single-prior estimator | 0.76 | 0.66 |
| Pooled estimator (saved) | 0.78 | 0.65 |

**Limitations.**
- **The prior is assumed, not measured.** It is not the real distribution of handwritten digits. The result depends on it: switching from one prior to the pooled set changed M by about 68%.
- **R² is not accuracy.** It measures how well the bridge recovers B's pre-activations under the assumed priors. Recovering about 78% of the variance should keep accuracy well above the 10% of a random bridge, but I can't say how close it gets to B's own 95–97%.
- **A sends only 15 live numbers.** B's first layer has 24 units, so some information it would normally get is lost before the bridge.

If you score it on real test images, I'd like to know the accuracy. That would show whether the prior was a reasonable guess.
